beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.

beats.trigger: Default to one agent with a good prompt.
beats.got: The default is one agent. Splitting adds handoffs and coordination cost, which is a relief to hear after the setup.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.

take_homes: Start with one agent. Split only when the agents need different access, speak different dialects or must disagree.
A synthesis can read convincingly and still be wrong, and nothing in this module checks it. I need a human check before I use the output.
What an agent can touch, not what it can write, is the risk. I need to talk to the DPO and the works council before pointing anything at employee data.

monday.move: Ask my DPO and the works council representative what rules apply before any agent reads people data. Then try one agent on my weekly people-metrics summary using non-personal data only.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner as reviewer
monday.when: Ask Monday morning, try the agent later in the week
monday.stop_condition: Stop if the data includes anything about named employees without clearance
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and DPO, and I have not asked yet.

misconception.why: The module never touched roles or headcount. It was about how to build agent systems, so my belief that agents replace headcount first stays as it was.

one_line: Good rule that one agent is the default and you split only for a reason, but it never said what it means for people, and I had to bring that question myself.
